analysis.one_liner: Lets patients sue HMOs and insurers for damages, including wrongful death, over denied care.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 16 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law (ERISA), people in employer-provided health plans generally cannot sue their HMO or insurer for damages when denied care — they can usually recover only the dollar value of the benefit that was withheld. This bill would have opened the door to state-court lawsuits for real damages, including wrongful death, when a plan's failure to provide benefits injures or kills a patient. It was referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and families covered by employer health plans who are injured, or lose a loved one, because a plan failed to provide promised benefits. They would gain the right to bring state-law damage suits — including wrongful death claims — against the insurers and companies administering the plan, rather than being limited to recovering the cost of the denied benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and families in employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Carves state-law damage suits — for personal injury, financial injury, or wrongful death — out of ERISA preemption when they arise from an employer health plan's failure to provide benefits.

Lets injured patients and surviving families sue the insurers and companies that provide or administer the health plan in state court and recover real damages, instead of being limited to the value of the denied benefit as under current ERISA rules.
Applies to causes of action arising after enactment, so families harmed by later denials of care would have a legal remedy.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care insurers, HMOs, and the companies administering employer health plans would face jury damages suits for denied or delayed care, including wrongful death claims. Employers would be mostly shielded — they could only be sued if they personally exercised authority to decide claims and that decision caused the harm — but insurers' litigation costs and payouts would partly flow into health premiums paid by employers and enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Exposing insurers and plans to malpractice-style jury awards would raise litigation costs that flow into health premiums, a cost employers and workers would partly bear.
The bill's employer carve-out — employers are liable only if they exercised discretionary authority over the denied claim — would create disputes over who actually made the decision to deny care.

It is a narrow remedy: it addresses only damage suits for failures to provide benefits and does nothing about other managed-care practices such as utilization review or coverage rules that fall short of outright denial.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concrete: a family whose loved one dies because a plan denied needed care would, for the first time, be able to seek actual damages rather than a check for the value of the denied service. The cost is higher litigation exposure for insurers and some premium pressure, though the employer carve-out made the bill more moderate than broad malpractice expansion. On balance the bill tilted toward patients, and its death left the ERISA shield for HMOs fully intact.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Education and the Workforce Committee, which sent it to its employer-employee subcommittee, and no hearing or vote ever happened before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Norwood, a Republican, introduced the bill on November 8, 1997, joined by original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Ganske, Sessions, and Paul and Democrats Edwards and Towns.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day, and on December 10, 1997, to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action was ever taken — the subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, and it never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers and HMOs are better off: the bill's death preserved their ERISA protection from damage lawsuits over denied care, while patients injured by benefit denials were left with no greater remedy than before.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican author with 16 cosponsors split 12 Democrats to 4 Republicans — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no roll-call record of who supported or opposed it.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped these companies of their ERISA shield against state-court damages suits — including wrongful death claims — for failing to provide promised health benefits. The bill's death preserved that shield, which caps their exposure at the value of a denied benefit no matter how much harm the denial causes.

The bill mostly left employers off the hook, allowing suits against them only when they personally decided the denied claim. Employer groups nonetheless opposed expanding liability in this area, fearing lawsuits and higher premium costs for job-based coverage.

The bill created a new malpractice-style cause of action in state court for harms from denied health benefits, expanding the pool of cases attorneys could bring on behalf of injured patients and grieving families.
